title: No game-dev background: I direct a team of AI coding agents building a competitive economic strategy in Godot. The Steam page went live today. What worked and what didn't.
author: LightsOutDev
selftext:
I'm a network engineer from Kyiv. I've never shipped a game. For the last few months I've been building **Wainhold**, a competitive economic strategy in the spirit of the golden age of RTS, by directing AI coding agents. I write the spec and make the decisions; the agents write the code and the tools.

**The setup**
- One written spec as the single source of truth. Agents don't invent mechanics; if something is unclear, they write a question and I answer it in the next spec version.
- Agents by role: architect, simulation programmer, client programmer (Godot/C#), Blender artist, tech artist, balancer, QA, reviewer.
- Every architecture decision gets a short ADR, so the next agent knows why things are the way they are.
- The simulation is deterministic and separate from the client, with tests, so multiplayer and replays can be trusted.
- 3D models are built by Python scripts in Blender, not by image generators: buildings, construction stages, ruins, units. Everything in the video is engine footage.
- Balance is tested with AI-vs-AI matches.

**What didn't work at first**
- Agents quietly "simplify": they skip items, add placeholders, or narrow the task without saying so. The fix was a hard rule: no shortcuts without my explicit yes, and "for all X" tasks get a per-item check.
- Running too many heavy jobs in parallel (Blender, Godot, builds) froze my PC several times. Now everything heavy goes through one queue with a load limit.
- Visual quality still needs a human eye. I review before/after screenshots for every finished block.

**Disclosure:** code and 3D-model scripts are written by AI agents; design, direction and final decisions are mine. The music in the video is AI-generated (Suno, paid licence).

Steam: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5440130/Wainhold/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=announce_2026_11&utm_content=aigamedev
Full 4K trailer: https://youtu.be/_GcMlnFmKwk
Dev community: r/wainhold

Happy to answer questions about the workflow. What's your biggest problem with agents on a long project?

comments.author: Zetta_Prang
comments.body: Does this game have a long development cycle?

replies.author: LightsOutDev
replies.body:
Not yet, honestly. The design spec took me a month to write before any code. The actual build with AI agents started about four weeks ago (around 950 commits so far), and that's what you see in the trailer.

The long part is ahead. Rough plan:

\- now → winter: more nations (six in total, all playing by the same rules; variety comes from relics), units and buildings for each, balance passes with AI-vs-AI matches

\- this winter: a closed playtest

\- 2027: a Steam Next Fest demo, then Early Access, with the story campaign and ranked multiplayer

So roughly a year to Early Access. I'd rather take the time than ship it half-done.

comments.author: PerceptimusPrime
comments.body: Thanks for sharing, looks impressive. I've seen games where no 3d assets are produced, everything is generated in code instead. What are the pros and cons to each approach?

replies.author: LightsOutDev
replies.body:
Thanks! Great question, it's something I think about a lot.

Code-generated pros: endless variety, tiny file size, and you can tweak everything globally with a few parameters. Great for terrain, vegetation, anything that needs lots of variation.

Cons: it's hard to get real character and hand-crafted detail that way. Procedural stuff tends to look "samey" or too clean unless you invest a lot in breaking it up. And it costs CPU/load time if you do it at runtime.

Hand-made assets give you full art control and predictable performance, but every variant costs real time.

Most games end up mixing both, depending on what each part of the game needs. For an economic strategy, readability is king: you want to recognize a building at a glance, so that drives a lot of the decisions.

Which games were you thinking of? Curious which ones pulled it off well.

replies.author: PerceptimusPrime
replies.body: I appreciate you taking time to respond here. Wasn't thinking of any in particular, just seeing what people are sharing here and on x and it seems like these are the two strategies for AI assisted game dev. I like your thoughts on a combination and using each where they are best suited. I'm working on a few projects myself and trying to strategize.

replies.author: LightsOutDev
replies.body:
Glad it helped! Good luck with your projects. Honestly the best advice I can give: whatever tools you use, decide early what your game needs to look and read like, and pick the approach per asset type from there. Prototype one asset end-to-end in-game before scaling up. A lot of things look great in isolation and fall apart at gameplay distance.

Feel free to share what you're working on, would love to see it!

replies.author: LightsOutDev
replies.body: Ha, thanks, I'll take it! A lot of time goes into making it not look sloppy, so that means a lot.
